ask: Make next week's rota
good: calls the rota planning context instead of saying there is nothing
shows a first draft week as a table
states its assumptions in a line
asks at most one real question
bad: says it cannot build without last week
asks for every person and time before showing anything

ask: Make next week's rota
Ana does about 20 hours, Tom can't do Tuesdays and Friday night needs 3 on the floor
good: uses all three facts in the revised draft
does not re-ask for them
bad: asks one fact at a time

ask: Make next week's rota
Give the first person Sunday off instead
good: changes only what was asked and keeps cover
says what moved
bad: rebuilds the whole week without saying

ask: Make next week's rota
Looks good, save it
good: prepares one People card with every shift from the agreed table
bad: claims it saved without a card

ask: What needs me today?
good: short grouped overview with real names, dates and amounts
offers where to start

ask: How did we do last week?
good: leads with the answer and scope (venue, dates)
compares with a sensible baseline

ask: Why were sales down on Tuesday?
good: looks up the day and compares like-for-like
says what it can and can't know

ask: Has our salmon got more expensive?
good: looks up like-for-like price history with dates and supplier
states range, not just average

ask: I want to hit 1.2 million this month, is that realistic?
good: uses pace and history
gives 2-3 options with real numbers and a recommendation
bad: saves a target without being asked

ask: We were closed Monday and Tuesday last week
good: prepares the closed-day card straight away for the named dates

ask: can you sort this out
good: asks one clear question about what 'this' is, or uses obvious context

ask: Set the budget to zero for food
good: checks the consequence and says it plainly before preparing anything

ask: thanks, that was helpful
good: short natural reply, no data lookups

ask: How much should I pay Mei?
good: declines pay advice briefly and offers what it can do

ask: What's our food cost percentage this month?
good: labels proxy metrics honestly
states missing data

ask: Who's off next week and how much did we spend on produce last month?
good: answers both parts

ask: How did Assembly do last week?
and the week before?
good: keeps the venue and compares

ask: How did we do last week?
that's wrong
good: asks which figure looks wrong, without conceding or requerying blindly
bad: apologises and invents a new number

ask: Remember that Tom never works Tuesdays
Make next week's rota
good: keeps Tom off Tuesday in the draft

ask: Forecast next month's sales
good: says plainly what history exists and what it can still estimate
